scripts.opening:opening:
[quietly] JAUNT: ONE YEAR AND A DAY. A Monday afternoon, 21 November 1904, at the Field houses on Prairie Avenue.

[short pause] Four stops between two houses: the father's and the son's. Marshall Field built one of the great stores of America and the biggest fortune in Chicago. His only surviving son lives two doors away. He is 36 and rich, and he has spent his whole life waiting to become the man his father is. [short pause] [ominous] Count the days with him. [short pause] Exactly one year and one day from now, a shot will be fired in the house at 1919.

[long pause] Start at the son's front door.
scripts.stop:son: [warmly] 1919 Prairie, the house of Mr. and Mrs. Marshall Field Jr. He bought it in 1890, and two years ago D. H. Burnham & Company built "a huge addition" for him. He married Albertine Huck, and they have three children: Henry, Marshall III and little Gwendolyn. [short pause] [tenderly] Look at them on the front walk this afternoon, the nurse with the youngest, the boys in their coats. [short pause] Everything a man could want is on this walk. [short pause] [quietly] Everything except his own name, which belongs to his father. [short pause] [wryly] He has been Junior all his life. Walk north, two doors up, to the house where the name lives.
scripts.stop:father: [measured] 1905 Prairie, the father's house, where the son grew up. It was "the first in Chicago to be completely wired for electricity". [short pause] [softly] There was a first son, Louis, who died a baby; this one lived, and was raised to inherit the store that taught America to "Give the lady what she wants". His father is "the wealthiest and most powerful businessman in Chicago". [short pause] [pointedly] The father does not hand over power. [short pause] He is planning to hand it past his son entirely: his will is going to put the fortune in trust for forty years, for the grandsons playing on the walk at 1919. [short pause] The son walks up to his father's door for his Monday call. Benson the butler lets him in. The house will be razed in 1955.
scripts.stop:talk: [conspiratorially] Up the street, look back at the two houses. [short pause] This is what the street sees: a dutiful son making his call. [short pause] [whispers] Here is what the street says, behind its curtains. The Levee is three blocks west, and the Everleigh Club on Dearborn Street counts the richest young men in Chicago among its guests; the gossips name Marshall Field Jr. among them. [short pause] Nobody has proved it, and nobody ever will. [short pause] [ominous] But a year and a day from now, the story they tell will be this: "The most popular story is that he was in fact shot at the Everleigh Club", and carried home to look like an accident. [short pause] Other people will say he did it himself. Go back to 1919.
scripts.stop:shot: [softly] 1919 again, as the afternoon goes. [short pause] The children have gone in. [long pause] [gravely] On Wednesday, 22 November 1905, one year and a day from this afternoon, Marshall Field Jr. will be shot in this house. [short pause] He will live five days. At Mercy Hospital he will say, "I shot myself with that revolver – accidentally". The coroner's jury will agree that he "had shot himself unintentionally while examining a revolver". [short pause] [lowering voice] Two reporters will be tipped that he spent the evening at the Everleigh Club; the sisters will deny it, and nobody will confirm it. The house will go on standing. [long pause] [softly] Look at the lit windows. The son of the richest man in Chicago is home for dinner, with one year and a day left.
scripts.ending:six-weeks: [gravely] End of the walk. Marshall Field Jr. died at Mercy Hospital on Monday 27 November 1905. [short pause] His father was 71 and had just remarried. On New Year's Day he went out to play golf, caught pneumonia, [short pause] and "Six weeks later, Marshall Field, Sr. was dead." [short pause] The fortune went in trust to the boys from the front walk at 1919, just as the will had planned. [long pause] [sadly] The son never got to be anything but Junior. [short pause] His sons got everything.
